meta.title: ACC 214 Cost Estimation Challenge
meta.subtitle: Three consulting engagements: account analysis, high-low, regression
meta.description: Reverse-engineered GameSpec fixture for public/acc214-cost-estimation/index.html. The richest game in the corpus and the one that forced three schema features: a cross-cutting modes[] construct, a resource meter with a payout rule, and narrativeNumbers with a checked prose quantifier.
meta.audience: undergraduate managerial accounting students, in class or self-paced after the lecture

sources.archivedAt: NOT ARCHIVED — the source file header cites "slides 12-47" with no pinned copy.

objectives.statement: Separate a mixed cost into its fixed and variable components by reading the underlying bill.
Build the cost equation Y = b + mX from an estimation method’s output.
Forecast cost at a stated activity level and state the relevant-range caveat.
Apply the high-low method using the highest and lowest ACTIVITY levels, not the highest and lowest costs.
Judge whether an estimated cost model is fit to budget on, using economic plausibility, goodness of fit and statistical significance.
Reason about how a change in a fixed or variable component moves the cost equation, within the relevant range.
Critique an estimation method by naming what its sample ignores and what an outlier does to it.

lines.text: Welcome to Rivera & Park. No time for a tour — Dover Manufacturing is on line two.
Corporate wants next year’s water budget by Friday. If my number is wrong, Facilities eats the difference.
Send over the bill. We will take it apart line by line — that is what account analysis means.
ENGAGEMENT #1 — separate fixed from variable, build the cost equation, forecast next year.

blocks.text: Your budget goes in at $31,200. The quarters roll by.
Actual for the year: $31,210 — your forecast was off by 0.03%.

narrativeNumbers.reason: Authored quarterly actual, illustrating variance around the forecast.
One quarter of the annual forecast ($31,200 / 4 = $7,800).
The sum of the four authored quarterly actuals, not a derivation of the forecast.
The stated forecast error, in percent.
The stated forecast error in percent, computed from the authored actuals.

lines.text: Next client is a referral. Zeffani — ceramic artist. Sells every mug she makes. And somehow, she is broke.
Sold-out markets. And my bank balance after seven years? Basically pottery dust.
You have seven years of cost data. Let us find the line hiding in it.
ENGAGEMENT #2 — use the high-low method to uncover where the money goes.

blocks.text: Knowing $12 a mug is variable and $3,000 a year is fixed, Zeffani reprices.
Turns out I was selling below variable cost at the small markets. I stopped doing the small markets.

lines.text: My intern ran a regression. I am about to put $200,000 of maintenance budget in front of the board on the strength of it.
Then before anyone signs anything, we run the three validity checks.
ENGAGEMENT #3 — judge whether the model is fit to budget on.

blocks.text: You present: plausible driver, R-squared 0.65, p 0.00086. The board locks next year’s maintenance budget on the model.
Every quarter lands within 2% of the model. The $200K bet pays off.

narrativeNumbers.reason: The "$200K bet" shorthand; the full figure is knowledge.params.boardBudgetAtRisk.

steps.prompt: Client briefing — Dover Manufacturing needs next year’s water budget by Friday.

steps.title: Sort the bill
steps.prompt: Sort each line of Dover’s water bill into the right cost type.
steps.caption: Account analysis means reading the actual bill to separate fixed from variable.

items.text: Meter base fee — $800 / month (charged even at zero usage)
items.why: Charged even at zero usage, so it does not vary with the driver.

items.text: Water usage charge — $2,000 / month (1,000 units used)

items.why: A fixed base plus a variable usage charge is a mixed cost.

steps.why: A mixed cost is a fixed base plus a variable rate.

steps.title: Variable rate
steps.prompt: What is the variable cost per unit of water?
steps.caption: The usage charge was $2,000 for 1,000 units this month.
steps.why: 2,000 / 1,000 = $2 per unit — the cost of each additional unit of water, i.e. the slope of the cost line.

steps.title: Assemble the equation
steps.prompt: Assemble the mixed-cost equation Y = b + mX.
steps.caption: Pull the fixed part (b) and the variable rate (m) from the bill.
steps.why: Y = 800 + 2X — an $800 fixed base plus $2 for every unit. With this equation you can predict the bill at any usage level X.

steps.title: Forecast next year
steps.prompt: Forecast next year’s water expense (usage drops 10%).
steps.caption: Annualize over 12 months. Fixed stays put; variable scales to 90%.
steps.why: $9,600 + $21,600 = $31,200. Only the variable part shrank with the 10% usage cut; the fixed meter fee did not move at all.

steps.prompt: One year later — the quarters roll by.

steps.title: Partner sign-off
steps.prompt: The city announces the meter base fee rises from $800 to $900 next year. What happens to Y = 800 + 2X?

options.label: The intercept shifts: Y = 900 + 2X. The slope does not change.
options.feedback: The base fee is the fixed part — the intercept b. The per-unit rate m is set by usage pricing and is untouched.

options.label: The slope rises to $2.25 per unit.
options.feedback: The base fee is not a per-unit charge, so it cannot change the slope.

options.label: Both the intercept and the slope increase.
options.feedback: Only the fixed base changed. The usage rate was not repriced.

options.label: Nothing changes.
options.feedback: A higher base fee raises the bill at every usage level — the intercept moves.

steps.why: A change in the fixed base moves the intercept, never the slope.

steps.title: Doubling volume
steps.prompt: Dover expects to double its water usage next year. Which statement is true?

options.label: Total fixed cost stays $9,600, so fixed cost per unit is cut in half.
options.feedback: Within the relevant range, fixed cost is constant in total, so per-unit fixed falls as volume rises.

options.label: Total fixed cost doubles along with usage.
options.feedback: Fixed cost is fixed in total, not per unit.

options.label: Variable cost per unit doubles to $4.
options.feedback: Variable cost is constant per unit; it is the TOTAL that scales.

options.label: Total variable cost stays the same.
options.feedback: Total variable cost scales with the driver.

steps.why: Fixed is constant in total; variable is constant per unit. Both statements only hold within the relevant range.

steps.prompt: Client briefing — Zeffani sells every mug she makes and is still broke.

steps.title: Pick the two points
steps.prompt: Pick the two points the high-low method uses.
steps.caption: Zeffani made mugs (X) at these costs (Y) over 7 years. Select exactly two points.

distractors.feedback: High-low reads the highest and lowest ACTIVITY level, not the highest and lowest cost.

steps.why: High-low uses the highest and lowest activity levels: 500 mugs and 100 mugs.

steps.title: Compute the slope
steps.prompt: Compute the slope (m), the variable cost per mug.
steps.caption: High point (500, $9,000) and low point (100, $4,200).
steps.why: m = 4,800 / 400 = $12 — the variable cost of making one more mug.

steps.title: Compute the intercept
steps.prompt: Compute the intercept (b), the fixed cost.
steps.caption: Use the high point: $9,000 total at 500 mugs, with a $12 variable rate.
steps.why: b = 9,000 - 12 x 500 = $3,000 of cost that is there whether or not a mug is made.

steps.title: Predict at 300 mugs
steps.prompt: Using Y = 12X + 3,000, what does it cost to make 300 mugs?

interaction.expectedExpr: ((p.potteryHighCost - p.potteryLowCost) / (p.potteryHighMugs - p.potteryLowMugs)) * p.potteryPredictMugs + (p.potteryHighCost - ((p.potteryHighCost - p.potteryLowCost) / (p.potteryHighMugs - p.potteryLowMugs)) * p.potteryHighMugs)

steps.prompt: One year later — Zeffani reprices.

steps.title: Partner sign-off
steps.prompt: What is the main weakness of the high-low method?

options.label: It uses only two observations, so an unusual year drives the whole equation.
options.feedback: High-low throws away every point between the extremes, and the extremes are exactly where outliers live.

options.label: It cannot handle mixed costs.
options.feedback: Separating a mixed cost is precisely what it does.

options.label: It requires a statistics package.
options.feedback: It needs only arithmetic — that is its appeal.

options.label: It gives the fixed cost but not the variable rate.
options.feedback: It gives both: the slope first, then the intercept.

steps.why: Two points, both at the extremes, is the whole sample high-low uses.

steps.title: The outlier question
steps.prompt: Year 2 shows 180 mugs at $4,000 — lower cost than year 1 at 100 mugs. What should you do?

options.label: Investigate it, but leave high-low on the true activity extremes.
options.feedback: High-low is defined on the activity extremes. An odd interior point is a reason to ask questions, not to redefine the method.

options.label: Use year 2 as the low point because it has the lowest cost.
options.feedback: That is the high-low-by-cost error: the method reads the ACTIVITY extremes.

options.label: Drop year 2 from the data set without asking why.
options.feedback: Deleting an inconvenient observation without a reason is not analysis.

steps.why: Investigate interior oddities; the method still reads the activity extremes.

steps.prompt: Client briefing — a $200K board budget rides on an intern’s regression.

steps.title: What regression minimises
steps.prompt: Drag the line until the squared errors are as small as you can get them.
steps.caption: Regression picks the line that minimises the sum of squared residuals.
steps.why: Ordinary least squares is exactly the line with the smallest sum of squared vertical distances.

steps.title: Validity check 1 — the driver
steps.prompt: The intern regressed maintenance cost on machine hours. Is the driver economically plausible?

options.label: Yes — machines that run more need more maintenance, so the causal story holds.
options.feedback: Economic plausibility comes first. A statistically strong relationship with no causal story is a coincidence you are about to budget on.

options.label: It does not matter, because R-squared is high.
options.feedback: R-squared measures fit, not causation. Plausibility is a separate, prior test.

options.label: No — cost can never be predicted from an activity measure.
options.feedback: That is what cost estimation is.

steps.title: Validity check 2 — goodness of fit
steps.prompt: R-squared is 0.65. Does the model clear the course threshold?

options.label: Yes — 0.65 is above the 0.30 rule of thumb, so the fit is acceptable.
options.feedback: R-squared of 0.65 means machine hours explain 65% of the variation in cost, comfortably above the 0.30 screening threshold.

options.label: No — anything below 0.90 is unusable.
options.feedback: A 0.90 bar would reject almost every real cost model.

options.label: R-squared cannot be judged without the p-value.
options.feedback: They are separate checks; both are run, neither replaces the other.

steps.why: R-squared 0.65 clears the 0.30 rule of thumb.

steps.title: Validity check 3 — significance
steps.prompt: t = 4.53 and p = 0.00086. What do you conclude about the machine-hours coefficient?

options.label: It is significant: |t| exceeds 1.96 and p is far below 0.05.
options.feedback: Both tests agree. The slope is distinguishable from zero.

options.label: It is not significant, because p is nearly zero.
options.feedback: A small p-value is evidence FOR the coefficient, not against it.

options.label: You cannot tell without the R-squared.
options.feedback: Significance of the coefficient is read from t and p.

steps.title: Assemble the regression equation
steps.prompt: Read the intercept and the machine-hours coefficient off the Excel output.

steps.title: The board number
steps.prompt: The plant plans 2,200 machine hours. What maintenance budget goes to the board?
steps.why: 14.98 x 2,200 + 8,773.72 = $41,729.72, which is the $41,730 the board locks in.

steps.prompt: The board meeting, and then the quarters.

steps.title: The board member’s question
steps.prompt: A board member asks: R-squared = 0.65 means machine hours explain 65% of cost variation. What about the other 35%?

options.label: Other drivers and random variation the model does not capture — which is why a relevant range and a review date matter.
options.feedback: Unexplained variation is not error to be embarrassed about; it is the honest width of the forecast.

options.label: Measurement mistakes in the data, which should be corrected until R-squared reaches 1.
options.feedback: A cost model that fits perfectly is usually overfitted, not correct.

options.label: Nothing — 65% means the model is right 65% of the time.
options.feedback: R-squared is variance explained, not a hit rate.

steps.why: The other 35% is everything the single driver does not capture.

softWrongByInteraction.numeric: Check the arithmetic and try again.
softWrongByInteraction.multi-blank: One of the blanks is off.

hints.text: Variable rate = variable dollars / units used.
b is the meter base fee charged even at zero usage; m is the per-unit rate you just found.
Slope = change in cost / change in activity.
Take the high point and strip out the variable part.
Excel labels them Intercept and the coefficient on your X variable.

assertions.describe: Dover variable rate $2/unit must appear in the graded text
Dover annual forecast must come to $31,200
High-low slope must be exactly $12 per mug
The high-low points must actually be the activity extremes of the seven-year table the student is shown
The board number must follow from the regression output on screen
The model the game teaches as valid must actually clear all three declared thresholds

extensions.textAlternative: Eight points scattered around a rising line. Two sliders set the slope and the intercept; a bar shows the sum of squared residuals, which shrinks as the line fits better. The best-fit values and the current sum of squared errors are printed as text beside the plot.

options.label: The line with the smallest sum of SQUARED vertical distances to the points.
options.feedback: That is the definition of ordinary least squares.

options.label: The line with the smallest total vertical distance, ignoring sign.
options.feedback: That is least absolute deviations — a different estimator.

options.label: The line that passes through the most points.
options.feedback: Regression is not interpolation; it can pass through none of them.

pedagogy.feedback: You found a line within 35% of the least-squares minimum, which is close enough to see what the criterion is doing.

debrief.headline: One-glance recap
debrief.body: Three engagements, three equations, three validity checks.
takeaways: Y = 800 + 2X — account analysis, read off the bill.
Y = 12X + 3,000 — high-low, from the activity extremes.
Y = 14.98X + 8,773.72 — regression, once it passed plausibility, fit and significance.
